title: Limb Plexuses & Peripheral Nerve Injuries
summary: Master the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses and predict the deficits that follow specific nerve injuries.

lessons.title: Brachial Plexus: Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords & Branches

levels.kid:
Imagine five garden hoses coming out of your neck. Before they reach your arm, they join, split and swap water, like a busy train junction. That junction is called the **brachial plexus**.

Why mix them up? Each arm muscle then gets wires from more than one hose. If one hose gets a small kink, the muscle can often still work a bit.

The junction has five stations in order: roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches. Some people remember them with a silly sentence: "Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer."

At the end come five big nerves. One of them is your funny bone nerve. That zingy feeling when you bump your elbow is that nerve being squished!
levels.hs:
The **brachial plexus** is a network of nerves that supplies almost all of the skin and muscles of the upper limb. A **plexus** is a place where nerve fibers merge and re-sort, so each final nerve carries fibers from several spinal levels.

It forms from the **ventral rami** (front branches) of spinal nerves **C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1**. From the neck to the armpit it passes through five stages:
- **Roots** (5): C5 to T1, emerging between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
- **Trunks** (3): upper (C5-C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8-T1), in the base of the neck.
- **Divisions** (6): each trunk splits into an anterior and a posterior division behind the clavicle (collarbone).
- **Cords** (3): lateral, posterior and medial, named for where they sit around the axillary artery in the armpit.
- **Branches**: the five big terminal nerves.

The five terminal branches are the **musculocutaneous**, **axillary**, **radial**, **median** and **ulnar** nerves. Posterior divisions supply muscles that extend the limb, such as the triceps. Anterior divisions supply flexors, such as the biceps and the forearm flexors.

Real example: the ulnar nerve runs behind the elbow, where it is only lightly covered. Hitting your "funny bone" squeezes this nerve and sends tingling into your little finger.
levels.college:
The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of **C5-T1**. It is called **prefixed** if C4 contributes substantially and **postfixed** if T2 does. A mnemonic for the sequence is "Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer": Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches.

**Anatomy by region**
- **Roots** lie in the posterior triangle of the neck, between anterior and middle scalenes.
- **Trunks**: upper (C5-6), middle (C7), lower (C8-T1). The lower trunk rests on the first rib, behind the subclavian artery.
- **Divisions** lie behind the clavicle. Anterior divisions serve flexor (ventral) compartments. Posterior divisions serve extensor (dorsal) compartments.
- **Cords** surround the second part of the axillary artery, deep to pectoralis minor:
  - **Lateral cord**: anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks (C5-7)
  - **Medial cord**: anterior division of the lower trunk (C8-T1)
  - **Posterior cord**: all three posterior divisions (C5-T1)

**Terminal branches**
- Lateral cord gives the **musculocutaneous nerve** (C5-7) and the **lateral root of the median nerve**.
- Medial cord gives the **ulnar nerve** (C8-T1) and the **medial root of the median nerve**.
- The two roots form the **median nerve** (C5-T1) in an "M" shape anterior to the axillary artery.
- Posterior cord gives the **axillary** (C5-6) and **radial** (C5-T1) nerves.

**Selected collateral branches**
- From the roots: **dorsal scapular** (C5) to the rhomboids, and **long thoracic** (C5-7) to serratus anterior.
- From the upper trunk: **suprascapular** (C5-6) to supraspinatus and infraspinatus, and the nerve to subclavius.
- From the lateral cord: **lateral pectoral** nerve.
- From the medial cord: **medial pectoral**, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm.
- From the posterior cord: upper and lower **subscapular** nerves, and the **thoracodorsal** nerve to latissimus dorsi.

The divisions carry no named branches. This is a common exam point.
levels.phd:
The plexus reflects limb development. In the limb bud, ventral (preaxial) muscle masses become flexors and dorsal (postaxial) masses become extensors. Motor axons from each segment bifurcate at the plexus to reach the appropriate mass. This dorsoventral choice is genetically specified. In motor neurons of the lateral motor column, **Lim1 (Lhx1)** expression drives axons dorsally. **Isl1** expression drives them ventrally. Guidance depends on **EphA4/ephrin-A** repulsion and **GDNF/Ret** signaling at the base of the limb (Kania and Jessell, 2000s). The anterior/posterior division split in adult anatomy is the morphological trace of this decision.

The segmental contribution of the terminal nerves shows a proximal-to-distal gradient. C5-6 dominate shoulder and elbow flexion. C7 contributes widely. C8-T1 control the intrinsic hand muscles. This is why myotome maps, such as the C5 deltoid, C6 wrist extensors, C7 triceps, C8 finger flexors and T1 interossei, are only approximations. Each muscle is multisegmental. Classic cadaver series (Kerr, 1918, 175 plexuses) documented that the textbook pattern holds in only a majority of specimens.

Topographic relations matter quantitatively. Roots lie within the interscalene groove. The plexus then crosses the costoclavicular space, a narrow passage between clavicle and first rib. It then lies posterior to pectoralis minor in the subcoracoid space. These are three potential compression points relevant to thoracic outlet syndrome.

Preganglionic versus postganglionic location is clinically central. The dorsal root ganglion sits in the intervertebral foramen, so a lesion proximal to it (an avulsion) leaves sensory axons attached to their cell bodies. In that case sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) are preserved despite anaesthesia. The **long thoracic** and **dorsal scapular** nerves arise directly from roots, so serratus anterior or rhomboid weakness localizes a lesion close to the spinal cord. Sympathetic fibers to the face leave at T1 via the white ramus. Ipsilateral Horner syndrome therefore signals a proximal lower-plexus injury.

Mechanistically, the C5 and C6 roots have dural attachments and fibrous anchoring to transverse processes. The lower roots lack these, which explains why C8-T1 are more prone to avulsion.
levels.expert:
For a clinician, the plexus is a localization problem. The questions are: root, trunk, cord or terminal nerve; pre- or postganglionic; and complete or partial. Bedside tests map onto each level:
- **Root level**: scapular winging (long thoracic), rhomboid weakness (dorsal scapular), hemidiaphragm palsy (phrenic, C3-5, sharing C5), Horner syndrome (T1).
- **Trunk level**: suprascapular involvement (weak external rotation and abduction initiation) places the lesion at or proximal to the upper trunk.
- **Cord level**: a posterior cord lesion hits the axillary, radial, thoracodorsal and subscapular nerves together. A radial nerve lesion in the spiral groove spares the deltoid and latissimus.

Electrodiagnosis is timed at about 3-4 weeks, after Wallerian degeneration has established. Paraspinal denervation on EMG indicates root-level injury, because posterior rami arise proximal to the plexus. Preserved SNAPs in an anaesthetic dermatome suggest preganglionic avulsion. **MR neurography** and CT myelography look for **pseudomeningoceles**, a marker of avulsion, although these do not perfectly predict avulsion.

Surgical implications follow directly. Postganglionic ruptures can be grafted, often with sural nerve. Avulsions cannot be repaired back to the cord by conventional means, so surgeons use **nerve transfers**. Examples are the **Oberlin transfer** (an ulnar fascicle to the biceps branch of the musculocutaneous nerve), spinal accessory to suprascapular, and a triceps branch of radial to axillary. Timing matters because denervated motor endplates degrade progressively. Reinnervation is generally sought within roughly 6-9 months of injury, and outcomes decline beyond about a year. Contralateral C7 transfer, first used for plexus avulsion, has been studied for spastic arm paralysis after stroke (Zheng et al., NEJM 2018).

In anaesthesia, the regional block chosen reflects plexus anatomy. **Interscalene** blocks target the roots and trunks, spare C8-T1 (ulnar), and almost invariably block the phrenic nerve. **Supraclavicular** blocks target the divisions and are compact. **Infraclavicular** and **axillary** blocks target the cords and branches; the musculocutaneous nerve often leaves the sheath early and may need a separate injection.

Open questions include optimal donor selection, cortical plasticity after transfer, and biologic adjuncts to speed axonal regeneration, such as electrical stimulation.

keyPoints: Brachial plexus = ventral rami of C5-T1
Sequence: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches
Trunks: upper C5-6, middle C7, lower C8-T1
Cords (lateral, posterior, medial) are named around the axillary artery
Terminal branches: musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar
Posterior divisions supply extensors; anterior divisions supply flexors

test.q: Which spinal nerve ventral rami usually form the brachial plexus?
test.explain: The plexus normally arises from C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1. Contribution from C4 makes it prefixed, and from T2 postfixed.

test.q: Which trunk is formed by C7 alone?
test.explain: The middle trunk is a continuation of C7. 'Lateral' is a cord name, not a trunk name.

test.q: The cords of the brachial plexus are named for their position relative to the:
test.explain: The lateral, posterior and medial cords surround the axillary artery.

test.q: Which cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves?
test.explain: The posterior cord, made of all three posterior divisions, gives the axillary and radial nerves.

test.q: The median nerve is formed by contributions from which cords?
test.explain: The lateral root and the medial root join to form the median nerve, often in an M shape.

test.q: Posterior divisions of the trunks mainly supply which kind of muscles?
test.explain: Posterior divisions reach the extensor (dorsal) compartments, such as the triceps. Anterior divisions reach the flexors.

test.q: Which nerve to serratus anterior arises directly from the roots?
test.explain: The long thoracic nerve (C5-7) arises from the roots. The thoracodorsal nerve comes from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi.

test.q: Where do the divisions of the brachial plexus lie?
test.explain: The divisions sit behind (posterior to) the clavicle. The roots lie between the scalenes, and the cords lie deep to pectoralis minor.

test.q: The ulnar nerve is a terminal branch of the:
test.explain: The ulnar nerve (C8-T1) comes from the medial cord.

test.q: Which terminal branch of the lateral cord supplies the biceps?
test.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-7) supplies the anterior arm flexors, including the biceps.

test.q: The plexus roots emerge between the anterior and middle ___ muscles.
test.explain: The roots pass through the interscalene groove.

test.q: The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper ___ of the plexus.
test.explain: The suprascapular nerve (C5-6) branches from the upper trunk.

kidTest.q: What is the brachial plexus?
choices: A large bone in the shoulder
A junction of nerves for the arm
kidTest.explain: It is a nerve junction where nerves join and split on their way to the arm.

kidTest.q: Where do these nerves come out from?
kidTest.explain: They leave the spinal cord in the neck.

kidTest.q: Why do the nerves mix together?
choices: So the arm bones grow longer
To make the arm feel heavier
kidTest.explain: Mixing gives each muscle backup wires from more than one nerve, so a small kink in one does not stop the muscle.

kidTest.q: How many big nerves come out at the end?
kidTest.explain: There are five big end branches.

kidTest.q: Bumping your 'funny b _ _ _' squishes a nerve.
kidTest.explain: The funny bone feeling comes from squishing the ulnar nerve at the elbow.

advancedTest.q: A patient has an anaesthetic hand dermatome but normal SNAPs there. The most likely lesion is:
choices: Damage to the cord within the axilla
Compression of the terminal nerve at the wrist
advancedTest.explain: If the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, the sensory axons stay attached to their cell bodies, so SNAPs persist even though the area is numb.

advancedTest.q: Weakness of the deltoid, latissimus dorsi and triceps together best localizes to the:
choices: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
advancedTest.explain: The posterior cord gives the axillary, thoracodorsal and radial nerves. A spiral groove lesion would spare the deltoid and latissimus.

advancedTest.q: Why does an interscalene block often fail to anaesthetize the ulnar territory?
choices: It acts on the cords below the clavicle
The ulnar nerve comes from the posterior cord
The ulnar nerve leaves the sheath early
It tends to spare the lower C8-T1 roots
advancedTest.explain: Interscalene blocks spread around the upper roots and trunks and often spare C8-T1, which supply the ulnar nerve.

advancedTest.q: Denervation found on EMG of the cervical paraspinal muscles implies the lesion lies:
choices: Proximal to where posterior rami branch off
Distal to the cords in the axilla
Within the divisions behind the clavicle
At the median nerve in the forearm
advancedTest.explain: Posterior rami arise before the plexus forms, so paraspinal denervation points to injury at the root level.

lessons.title: Upper Limb Nerve Lesions: Erb, Klumpke, Wrist Drop & Claw Hand

levels.kid:
Your arm has nerves like electric wires. They carry messages from your spinal cord to your muscles. The wires leave your neck in a bundle, then split into smaller wires for each part of your arm.

If one wire gets hurt, only the muscles on that wire stop working. That makes a special pattern:
- If the top wires are stretched, the arm hangs down and the palm faces backward, like a waiter sneaking a tip.
- If the bottom wires are stretched, the hand curls up like a claw.
- If the wire on the back of the arm is hurt, the wrist flops down and cannot lift up.

Doctors look at these patterns to figure out which wire was hurt.
levels.hs:
The **brachial plexus** is a network of nerves made from spinal nerves C5 to T1. It supplies the shoulder, arm and hand. Because each nerve controls certain muscles, damage creates a recognizable pattern of weakness.

Four classic injuries:
- **Erb palsy (upper plexus, C5-C6)**: caused when the head and shoulder are forced apart, as in a hard birth or a motorbike fall. The shoulder can't lift the arm sideways and the elbow can't bend well. The arm hangs turned inward with the forearm pronated. This is the "**waiter's tip**" position.
- **Klumpke palsy (lower plexus, C8-T1)**: caused when the arm is pulled upward, like grabbing a branch while falling. The small muscles of the hand fail, giving a **claw hand**. If the T1 root is torn near the spinal cord, the eyelid on that side may droop (**Horner syndrome**).
- **Wrist drop (radial nerve)**: often from a fracture of the middle of the humerus, where the radial nerve wraps around the bone. The wrist and finger extensors fail.
- **Claw hand (ulnar nerve)**: the ring and little fingers curl because the small hand muscles that straighten them are weak.

Example: a newborn after a difficult shoulder delivery holds one arm limp in waiter's tip position. That is Erb palsy, and many babies recover over months.
levels.college:
Lesion localization rests on knowing which **roots** and **peripheral nerves** supply each muscle. Ask two questions: is the deficit a root pattern or a single-nerve pattern, and how far along the nerve does the damage sit?

**Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6 upper trunk)**
- Mechanism: an increased angle between neck and shoulder (shoulder dystocia, falls onto the shoulder).
- Lost: deltoid and supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus (lateral rotation), biceps and brachialis (elbow flexion and supination).
- Posture: arm adducted, medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated ("waiter's tip"). Sensory loss covers the lateral arm and forearm.

**Klumpke palsy (C8-T1 lower trunk)**
- Mechanism: forced arm abduction above the head. A cervical rib or Pancoast tumour can also compress the lower trunk.
- Lost: intrinsic hand muscles and the long finger flexors. The result is a claw hand with numbness on the medial forearm and hand.
- A T1 root avulsion interrupts sympathetic outflow and causes Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

**Radial nerve: wrist drop**
- At the **spiral groove** (midshaft humerus fracture, "Saturday night palsy"): wrist and finger extensors are paralysed, and there is numbness over the dorsal first web space. Triceps is usually spared because its branches leave the nerve higher up.
- At the axilla (crutch palsy): triceps is lost as well.
- A posterior interosseous nerve lesion causes finger drop without true wrist drop, with no sensory loss.

**Ulnar nerve: claw hand**
- The medial two lumbricals and the interossei are weak. The ring and little fingers hyperextend at the MCP joints and flex at the IP joints.
- **Ulnar paradox**: a lesion at the wrist causes worse clawing than one at the elbow. An elbow lesion also paralyses the medial flexor digitorum profundus, so the fingers flex less.
- **Froment sign** reveals adductor pollicis weakness.
levels.phd:
Clinical patterns reflect the anatomy of root attachment and the biology of nerve repair.

**Pre- vs postganglionic injury.** The dorsal root ganglion lies in the intervertebral foramen. In a **preganglionic avulsion**, the root is torn from the cord proximal to the ganglion. Sensory axons stay connected to their cell bodies, so the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) is preserved even though the patient feels nothing. In a postganglionic lesion, the distal sensory axons degenerate and the SNAP is lost.

Other clues to avulsion:
- Paralysis of the serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) and the rhomboids (dorsal scapular nerve), whose branches arise very close to the roots.
- Horner syndrome.
- Pseudomeningoceles on imaging.

The C5 and C6 roots resist avulsion better than C8 and T1. They are tethered by transverse-process ligaments, whereas the lower roots have weak foraminal support. Lower roots therefore tend to avulse, while upper injuries are more often extraforaminal ruptures.

**Seddon/Sunderland grading.** Nerve injuries are graded by how much of the nerve's structure survives:
- **Neurapraxia**: focal demyelination with a conduction block and no axonal degeneration. Saturday night palsy usually behaves this way and recovers in weeks.
- **Axonotmesis**: the axons are interrupted but the endoneurial tubes are intact. **Wallerian degeneration** clears the distal axon over days. Regrowth then proceeds at about 1 mm/day (often quoted as 1 inch per month).
- **Neurotmesis**: the whole nerve is disrupted. It needs surgical repair.

Sunderland subdivides axonotmesis by endoneurial, perineurial and epineurial involvement (grades 2-4).

**Neonatal brachial plexus palsy.** It is linked to shoulder dystocia, although cases also follow caesarean delivery, suggesting intrauterine forces contribute. Most infants with upper-plexus injury recover substantially. Narakas classification and recovery of biceps function by about 3-6 months help guide decisions about surgery.

**Ulnar claw mechanics.** Without the lumbricals and interossei, the extensor digitorum pulls the MCP joints into extension. Its pull is then not transmitted through the extensor hood to the IP joints, which flex under FDP tone. In median-plus-ulnar lesions, all four fingers claw. A "benediction" posture on attempted fist-making instead indicates a proximal median lesion and must not be confused with ulnar clawing.
levels.expert:
Practical localization depends on targeted examination, electrodiagnostic timing and knowing when repair windows close.

**Examination pearls**
- Test **rhomboids, serratus anterior and spinati** to place a lesion at the root, trunk or more distal level.
- **Wartenberg sign** (little-finger abduction) and **Froment sign** are early indicators of ulnar weakness.
- In wrist drop, splint the wrist before testing finger abduction. Interossei appear falsely weak when the wrist is flexed. This catches students out.
- A C7 radiculopathy can mimic radial palsy, but triceps and wrist flexors (also C7) are weak too. A central lesion may present as a "pseudo-radial" hand.

**Electrodiagnostic timing.** Fibrillation potentials appear roughly 2-3 weeks after axonal injury. Early electromyography can therefore underestimate damage, although it helps confirm continuity. Serial studies and the appearance of nascent motor units track regeneration. CT myelography or high-resolution MR neurography identify root avulsions. Nerve ultrasound is increasingly used for lesions in continuity.

**Surgical strategy.** Neuromuscular junctions and denervated muscle degrade progressively, and motor endplates are often considered unsalvageable after about 12-18 months. This makes timing critical. Options include:
- **Nerve grafting** for ruptures (commonly using the sural nerve).
- **Nerve transfers** for avulsions: the spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve; the **Oberlin transfer** (ulnar fascicle to the biceps branch); triceps branch to the axillary nerve; and the anterior interosseous nerve to the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve, which can be done supercharged end-to-side.
- **Tendon transfers** for established radial palsy (for example pronator teres to ECRB).

Transfers shorten the regeneration distance and are now standard for proximal injuries.

**Frontiers and open questions**
- Brief low-frequency **electrical stimulation** of the nerve at the time of repair accelerates axonal outgrowth in trials.
- Contralateral C7 transfer has been explored, including for spastic arm paralysis after stroke.
- Neonatal timing remains debated: early versus delayed exploration, and the best recovery markers.
- Chronic neuropathic pain after avulsion can be treated with dorsal root entry zone (DREZ) lesioning, a classic neurosurgical procedure.
- The weak point is central: cortical remapping and recovery are less predictable after avulsion than after peripheral repair.

keyPoints: Erb palsy: C5-C6 upper trunk injury giving the waiter's tip posture
Klumpke palsy: C8-T1 lower trunk injury giving claw hand, sometimes with Horner syndrome
Midshaft humerus fracture can injure the radial nerve in the spiral groove, causing wrist drop
Ulnar nerve lesions cause clawing of the ring and little fingers; distal lesions claw worse
A preserved SNAP with lost sensation points to a preganglionic root avulsion
Seddon grades: neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis; regrowth is about 1 mm per day

test.q: Which roots are injured in Erb palsy?
test.explain: Erb palsy involves the upper trunk, formed by C5 and C6. C8-T1 injury is Klumpke palsy.

test.q: The 'waiter's tip' posture includes:
test.explain: Loss of the abductors, lateral rotators and biceps leaves the arm adducted, medially rotated and pronated.

test.q: Which mechanism typically causes Klumpke palsy?
choices: Forced upward pull of the arm
Pressure on the wrist from a cast
test.explain: Forced abduction above the head stretches the lower trunk (C8-T1).

test.q: Ptosis and miosis with a Klumpke-type injury suggest:
test.explain: T1 avulsion interrupts sympathetic outflow to the face, causing Horner syndrome.

test.q: A midshaft humerus fracture most often injures which nerve?
test.explain: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus and is vulnerable there.

test.q: With a radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove, triceps is usually:
test.explain: The branches to triceps leave the radial nerve above the groove.

test.q: The ulnar paradox states that clawing is worse with a lesion at the:
test.explain: An elbow lesion also weakens the medial FDP, so the fingers flex less and the claw looks milder.

test.q: Which fingers claw in an ulnar nerve lesion?
test.explain: The medial two lumbricals are ulnar-supplied, so the ring and little fingers claw.

test.q: A posterior interosseous nerve lesion produces:
test.explain: The PIN is purely motor and spares the radial wrist extensor, giving finger drop without true wrist drop.

test.q: Clawing of the hand caused by a lower trunk injury is called ___ palsy.
test.explain: Klumpke palsy affects C8-T1.

test.q: What sign tests adductor pollicis weakness by gripping paper between the thumb and index finger?
test.explain: The patient compensates with flexor pollicis longus, flexing the thumb tip.

test.q: Erb palsy affects the upper ___ of the brachial plexus.
test.explain: C5 and C6 join to form the upper trunk.

kidTest.q: What do arm nerves do?
kidTest.explain: Nerves are like wires carrying messages.

kidTest.q: If the top nerves are stretched, the arm looks like:
kidTest.explain: This is called the waiter's tip position.

kidTest.q: If the bottom nerves are stretched, the hand looks like:
kidTest.explain: The fingers curl up into a claw shape.

kidTest.q: When the wire on the back of the arm is hurt, the wrist:
kidTest.explain: This is called wrist drop.

kidTest.q: Nerves act like electric w _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages like wires carry electricity.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a flail arm with absent sensation, but SNAPs are normal. The likely lesion is:
choices: Distal axonotmesis of the radial nerve
advancedTest.explain: If the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, sensory axons stay connected to their cell bodies, so the SNAP survives.

advancedTest.q: Why do C8-T1 roots avulse more often than C5-C6?
choices: They have a much thicker epineurium
They lie directly behind the clavicle
They carry many more motor fibres
advancedTest.explain: The upper roots are tethered by transverse-process ligaments; the lower roots are not.

advancedTest.q: Why is a nerve transfer preferred over grafting for a proximal avulsion?
choices: It restores sensation before motor function
It shortens the regeneration distance to muscle
It avoids the need for electrodiagnostic testing
advancedTest.explain: Muscle endplates degrade over time. A transfer close to the target muscle beats that clock.

advancedTest.q: EMG done 5 days after a nerve injury shows no fibrillations. What is the best interpretation?
choices: It is too early to see denervation
The injury is a confirmed neurapraxia
advancedTest.explain: Fibrillation potentials appear about 2-3 weeks after axonal injury, so their absence at day 5 rules nothing out.

lessons.title: Lumbosacral Plexus Organization

levels.kid:
Your spinal cord is like a big power cable running down your back. Wires called **nerves** leave it to bring messages to your body.

The nerves for your legs leave from your lower back. Before they go to the legs, they meet and mix, like roads joining at a busy roundabout. This meeting place is called a **plexus**.

There are two parts. The top part, the **lumbar plexus**, sends nerves to the front of your thigh. They help you kick a ball. The bottom part, the **sacral plexus**, makes the biggest nerve in your body, the **sciatic nerve**. It is about as thick as your thumb! It runs down the back of your leg and helps you walk, run and wiggle your toes.
levels.hs:
A **plexus** is a network where spinal nerves join, split and rejoin before forming named nerves. The lower limb gets its nerves from the **lumbosacral plexus**, which uses the front branches (**anterior rami**) of spinal nerves T12 to S4.

It has two parts:
- The **lumbar plexus** (T12-L4) forms inside the **psoas major** muscle on the back wall of the abdomen. Its two big branches are the **femoral nerve** (L2-L4), which straightens the knee by supplying the quadriceps, and the **obturator nerve** (L2-L4), which pulls the thigh inward by supplying the adductor muscles.
- The **sacral plexus** (L4-S4) lies on the **piriformis** muscle at the back of the pelvis. Its main branch is the **sciatic nerve** (L4-S3), the largest nerve in the body.

The two parts are connected by the **lumbosacral trunk**, made of part of L4 and all of L5. It drops into the pelvis to join the sacral roots.

A real example: a large herniated disc or a pelvic tumor can press on the lumbosacral trunk. That can weaken the muscles that lift the foot even though no single leg nerve was cut. Knowing the plexus helps doctors find where the damage really is.
levels.college:
The lumbosacral plexus is built from the **anterior rami of T12-S4**. It has the same logic as the brachial plexus: rami split into **anterior (ventral) divisions**, which supply flexor/adductor territory, and **posterior (dorsal) divisions**, which supply extensor/abductor territory.

**Lumbar plexus (L1-L4, often a twig from T12)**, formed within psoas major:
- **Iliohypogastric** and **ilioinguinal** (L1): lower abdominal wall, groin skin.
- **Genitofemoral** (L1-L2): pierces the front of psoas; its genital branch supplies the cremaster.
- **Lateral femoral cutaneous** (L2-L3): skin of the lateral thigh.
- **Femoral** (L2-L4, posterior divisions): emerges lateral to psoas and passes under the inguinal ligament. It supplies iliacus, pectineus, sartorius and quadriceps, and gives the **saphenous nerve**.
- **Obturator** (L2-L4, anterior divisions): emerges medial to psoas and leaves through the obturator canal to the adductors and gracilis.

**Sacral plexus (L4-S4)**, on piriformis, behind the internal iliac vessels:
- **Superior gluteal** (L4-S1): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae.
- **Inferior gluteal** (L5-S2): gluteus maximus.
- **Sciatic** (L4-S3): really two nerves in one sheath. The **tibial** part comes from anterior divisions and the **common fibular (peroneal)** part from posterior divisions. It usually leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.
- **Posterior femoral cutaneous** (S1-S3).
- **Pudendal** (S2-S4): perineum and external sphincters.
- Small direct branches to piriformis, obturator internus/superior gemellus, and quadratus femoris/inferior gemellus.

The **lumbosacral trunk** (L4-L5) links the two parts. Note the theme: posterior divisions supply extensors (femoral to quadriceps, common fibular to dorsiflexors), while anterior divisions supply flexors and adductors (obturator, tibial).
levels.phd:
The division logic of the lumbosacral plexus is set during development. The limb bud rotates medially, about 90 degrees, so the embryonic dorsal (extensor) muscle mass ends up facing anterior in the thigh and leg. This is why the dorsal-division femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh. The tibial and common fibular nerves stay separate from their roots onward, and in roughly 10-15% of people they split high in the pelvis. In those cases the common fibular part often passes through or above piriformis. Classic dissection series, beginning with Beaton and Anson, sorted these piriformis-sciatic relationships into types.

**Hybrid and anomalous elements:**
- An **accessory obturator nerve** (L3-L4) occurs in about 8-30% of people, depending on the series. It crosses the superior pubic ramus rather than using the obturator canal and can supply pectineus.
- The plexus can be **prefixed** (shifted up a segment, with T12 contributing more and the trunk carrying L3-L4) or **postfixed** (shifted down). The **furcal nerve**, usually L4, splits between femoral, obturator and lumbosacral trunk and marks the boundary. This shifting changes which segmental level a given root lesion affects.
- **Pectineus** often gets supply from both the femoral and obturator nerves, consistent with its position between the two division territories.

**Relations that matter for physiology and injury:** the lumbosacral trunk crosses the sacral ala and pelvic brim with little padding. Here it can be compressed by the fetal head during labor or injured in sacral fractures. The genitofemoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves show many branching variants. The inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus receives **pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4)**, the parasympathetic outflow. The sacral plexus itself gets gray rami from the sympathetic trunk, so sudomotor and vasomotor fibers travel to the limb with somatic branches.

The overlap between dermatomes and myotomes is substantial. Most lower-limb muscles receive two or three roots, so single-root lesions cause partial weakness in several nerve territories. Peripheral nerve lesions instead produce deficits confined to one nerve's territory, while plexus lesions affect several nerves. This difference underlies localization by electrodiagnosis.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the main task is telling a **lumbosacral plexopathy** apart from **radiculopathy** and **mononeuropathy**, because these mimic one another and are treated very differently.

Localization pearls:
- **Hip adduction** (obturator) plus **knee extension** (femoral) weakness together suggests L2-L4 root or lumbar plexus disease. Isolated knee extension weakness suggests femoral neuropathy.
- **Hip abduction/internal rotation** (superior gluteal) and **foot inversion** (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) are spared in common fibular neuropathy but affected in L5 radiculopathy and lumbosacral trunk lesions. Testing them separates a fibular head problem from a proximal one.
- **Paraspinal denervation** on EMG means the lesion is at the root, because the dorsal rami branch off before the plexus. Plexopathy spares the paraspinals. **Sensory nerve action potentials** (sural, superficial fibular, saphenous) are reduced in plexopathy but preserved in radiculopathy, since the lesion is distal to the dorsal root ganglion.

Causes by setting:
- **Retroperitoneal hematoma** in iliacus or psoas, often during anticoagulation, compresses the femoral nerve or lumbar plexus. Expect groin pain, hip flexed for comfort, and quadriceps weakness.
- **Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy** (Bruns-Garland, diabetic amyotrophy) is a painful, asymmetric, proximal syndrome with weight loss. Biopsies show microvasculitis. It largely recovers, although slowly.
- **Neoplastic** plexopathy (colorectal, cervical, prostate cancer, lymphoma) is usually painful. **Radiation** plexopathy is often painless and may show myokymia on EMG.
- **Obstetric**: lumbosacral trunk compression at the pelvic brim produces foot-drop-like weakness after labor.

**Surgical relevance:** the **lateral transpsoas (XLIF) approach** to the lumbar spine puts the lumbar plexus at risk. The plexus lies more anteriorly within psoas at lower levels, especially L4-L5, so surgeons use a 'safe zone' and real-time triggered EMG. Postoperative thigh numbness and weakness of hip flexion are common, usually temporary, complications. Iliac crest bone harvest and anterior hip approaches threaten the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing **meralgia paresthetica**.

Open questions include better high-resolution MR neurography for imaging plexus lesions, and the role of immunotherapy in diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy, which is still unproven in randomized trials.

keyPoints: The lumbosacral plexus forms from anterior rami of T12-S4
Lumbar plexus (L1-L4) forms within psoas major; sacral plexus (L4-S4) lies on piriformis
Femoral (L2-L4, posterior divisions) supplies quadriceps; obturator (L2-L4, anterior divisions) supplies adductors
The lumbosacral trunk (L4-L5) links the lumbar and sacral plexuses
Sciatic nerve (L4-S3) = tibial (anterior divisions) + common fibular (posterior divisions)
EMG paraspinals and sensory potentials help separate plexopathy from radiculopathy

advancedTest.q: A patient has weak ankle dorsiflexion plus weak foot inversion and hip abduction, with normal paraspinal EMG and a reduced superficial fibular sensory potential. The best localization is:
choices: Lumbosacral trunk or sacral plexus lesion
L5 root compression in the foramen
Common fibular nerve at the fibular head
Femoral nerve under the inguinal ligament
advancedTest.explain: Inversion and hip abduction weakness rule out a fibular head lesion. Spared paraspinals and a reduced sensory potential point past the dorsal root ganglion, so the lesion is in the plexus rather than the root.

advancedTest.q: Why does the dorsal-division femoral nerve end up supplying the anterior thigh?
choices: The femoral nerve crosses over to the front during adulthood
Anterior rami consistently supply anterior muscles in each limb
Medial rotation of the limb bud turns the dorsal mass to face forward
The quadriceps originate as ventral muscles that later migrate back
advancedTest.explain: The lower limb bud rotates medially during development, so the embryonic dorsal (extensor) compartment faces anteriorly in the adult.

advancedTest.q: In a prefixed lumbosacral plexus, what would you expect?
choices: The obturator nerve takes over femoral nerve territory
Root levels for each nerve shift upward, changing root localization
The sciatic nerve reliably divides high up inside the pelvis
The plexus shifts one segment lower, with S4 contributing more

advancedTest.q: During a lateral transpsoas approach at L4-L5, why is plexus injury a particular concern?
choices: The obturator canal opens directly onto the L4-L5 disc
Psoas is absent at L4-L5, leaving the plexus exposed
The sacral plexus crosses the disc space at L4-L5
The plexus lies more anteriorly within psoas at lower lumbar levels
advancedTest.explain: The lumbar plexus moves anteriorly within psoas at lower levels, narrowing the safe zone. Triggered EMG monitoring is used for this reason.

lessons.title: Lower Limb Nerve Lesions: Foot Drop & Trendelenburg Gait

levels.kid:
Walking looks easy, but your brain sends messages down long wires called **nerves** to tell each leg muscle when to pull.

One nerve wraps around the outside of your knee, just under the skin. If it gets squished or hurt, the muscles that lift the front of your foot stop working. The toes flop down and drag, so the person lifts the knee high like they are stepping over a puddle. Doctors call this **foot drop**.

Another nerve works muscles on the side of your hip. They keep your hips level, like a seesaw held flat. If that nerve is hurt, the hip on the other side dips down with every step. That wobble is called a **Trendelenburg gait**.

By watching how someone walks, doctors can guess which wire is hurt.
levels.hs:
Many lower limb nerve injuries show up as a recognizable way of walking, so a careful look at someone's **gait** (walking pattern) can point to the damaged nerve.

**Foot drop** means a person cannot lift the front of the foot (**dorsiflexion**). The muscles that do this sit in the front of the leg and are supplied by the **deep fibular (peroneal) nerve**, a branch of the **common fibular nerve**. The common fibular nerve wraps around the **neck of the fibula** just under the skin, which makes it the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb. Fractures, tight casts, crossing the legs for long periods, or a knee injury can damage it. To stop the toes from catching, the person lifts the knee high. This is a **steppage gait**, and the foot may slap down with each step.

**Trendelenburg gait** comes from weakness of the **gluteus medius and minimus**, supplied by the **superior gluteal nerve**. While you stand on one leg, these muscles pull the pelvis level. If they are weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite side. Example: an injection placed badly in the buttock injures the right superior gluteal nerve. When the patient stands on the right leg, the left hip sags. This is a positive **Trendelenburg sign**. Patients often lean their trunk over the weak side to compensate.
levels.college:
Lower limb nerve lesions are best predicted by mapping each nerve to its muscles and skin territory, then asking what fails during gait.

**Common fibular nerve (L4-S2)**, from the sciatic nerve, winds around the fibular neck and splits into:
- **Deep fibular**: anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, fibularis tertius). Loss gives weak dorsiflexion and toe extension, plus numbness of the first dorsal web space.
- **Superficial fibular**: lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis). Loss gives weak eversion and numbness of most of the dorsum of the foot.

A common fibular lesion causes foot drop with an inverted, plantarflexed foot, a high-stepping (steppage) gait, and foot slap. Inversion is preserved because tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve. That detail helps separate a fibular nerve lesion from an L5 root lesion.

**Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1)** supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae. These muscles abduct the hip and, more importantly, stabilize the pelvis during single-leg stance. A lesion gives a positive **Trendelenburg sign**: the pelvis drops on the side opposite the lesion when the patient stands on the affected limb. In a **compensated** gait, the trunk lurches toward the affected side. This moves the centre of mass over the hip and shortens the lever arm the abductors must work against.

**Other key lesions:**
- **Inferior gluteal nerve**: gluteus maximus is weak, causing difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs and a backward trunk lurch.
- **Tibial nerve**: loss of plantarflexion and inversion, weak toe flexion, numbness of the sole. Patients cannot rise on their toes.
- **Femoral nerve**: weak knee extension (quadriceps), lost patellar reflex, and the knee may buckle.
- **Obturator nerve**: weak adduction and medial thigh numbness.

Gluteal intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant or ventrogluteal site to avoid the sciatic and gluteal nerves.
levels.phd:
Localizing foot drop is a classic exercise in separating root, plexus, sciatic and fibular lesions, because each predicts a different pattern of muscle weakness and reflex change.

- **Common fibular neuropathy at the fibular head**: dorsiflexion and eversion are weak, while inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve, L5) and hip abduction are spared. Ankle and knee reflexes are normal.
- **L5 radiculopathy** (often from a posterolateral L4-L5 disc herniation compressing the traversing L5 root): dorsiflexion and toe extension are weak, but inversion is also weak, and so is hip abduction (gluteus medius, L5). A radicular pain pattern supports the diagnosis.
- **Sciatic neuropathy** (for example after hip arthroplasty or posterior hip dislocation): the fibular division is preferentially affected, which is attributed to its fewer, larger fascicles with less connective tissue and its tethering at the sciatic notch and fibular neck. The hamstrings (short head of biceps femoris is fibular-innervated) and tibial muscles are also involved.
- **Lumbosacral plexopathy** produces multi-nerve deficits that do not respect a single root.

The Trendelenburg sign reflects a mechanics problem. In single-leg stance, body weight acts medial to the hip, producing an adduction moment. The abductors work with a lever arm roughly half that of body weight, so they must generate a force of about twice body weight. Weakness therefore shows up dramatically in stance. A positive sign is not specific to the superior gluteal nerve: hip osteoarthritis, a shortened femoral neck, coxa vara, developmental dysplasia, and abductor tendon tears all reduce effective abductor force. L5 radiculopathy can also produce it.

Electrodiagnosis refines localization. Nerve conduction studies across the fibular head can show focal **conduction block** or slowing, consistent with demyelination. EMG of the **short head of biceps femoris** distinguishes sciatic from fibular lesions, because its branch arises above the knee. Abnormal paraspinal muscles point to a root lesion. The **Seddon** classification (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis) frames prognosis: neurapraxia usually recovers over weeks, whereas axonal injury depends on regrowth at roughly 1 mm per day.
levels.expert:
Clinically, foot drop is a symptom with a broad differential, and the stakes of mislocalizing it are real. Before attributing it to the fibular nerve, examine inversion, hip abduction and reflexes. Then ask whether the problem is truly lower motor neuron. Central causes include a parasagittal (falx) meningioma or a stroke affecting the leg area of the motor cortex. Brisk reflexes, an upgoing plantar response or spasticity should redirect you toward imaging the brain or spinal cord. Painless bilateral foot drop suggests a length-dependent polyneuropathy or motor neuron disease rather than compression.

Common iatrogenic and positional causes of common fibular palsy:
- Lateral positioning or lithotomy stirrups pressing on the fibular head.
- Tight casts, splints or compression devices.
- Rapid weight loss, which removes protective fat (for example after bariatric surgery).
- Knee dislocation, particularly posterolateral injuries, which carry a high rate of fibular nerve traction injury.
- Ganglion cysts. **Intraneural ganglia** track from the superior tibiofibular joint along the articular branch. Spinner's unifying articular theory reshaped surgery: ligating the articular branch reduces recurrence.

Management depends on mechanism. Positional neurapraxia is managed with padding, removing the compression and an **ankle-foot orthosis (AFO)**. Clinicians commonly explore a non-recovering lesion at about three months, because motor endplates degrade with prolonged denervation and late repair performs poorly. Options include neurolysis, nerve grafting, and **nerve transfers** such as tibial nerve fascicles to the deep fibular motor branch. Results of these transfers are mixed. **Tibialis posterior tendon transfer** through the interosseous membrane restores active dorsiflexion when nerve recovery fails.

For Trendelenburg gait, the superior gluteal nerve is at risk in lateral (direct transgluteal) hip approaches. The nerve runs only a few centimetres above the greater trochanter between gluteus medius and minimus, and splitting medius too far proximally can damage it. Gluteus medius tendon tears are increasingly recognized as a cause of "greater trochanteric pain syndrome" with abductor weakness, and are now repaired endoscopically.

Open questions include optimal timing of exploration, the value of electrical stimulation to accelerate regeneration, and how well nerve transfers compare with tendon transfers for restoring natural gait.

keyPoints: Common fibular nerve wraps the fibular neck and is the most often injured lower limb nerve
Deep fibular loss causes foot drop and a high-stepping (steppage) gait
Spared inversion suggests a fibular nerve lesion; weak inversion suggests L5 radiculopathy
Superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, the pelvic stabilizers
Positive Trendelenburg sign: pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak abductors
Upper motor neuron signs with foot drop point to a central cause

test.explain: The tibial nerve supplies the calf plantarflexors such as gastrocnemius and soleus.

test.explain: Leaning over the weak hip moves the centre of mass over it and reduces the work the abductors must do.

lessons.title: Entrapment Neuropathies: Carpal, Cubital & Tarsal Tunnels

levels.kid:
Nerves are like long wires that carry messages between your brain and your hands and feet. Most of the time they have plenty of room.

But in a few places, a nerve has to squeeze through a narrow tunnel made of bone and tough bands. If the tunnel gets crowded or swollen, the nerve gets pinched, like a garden hose with a foot standing on it.

A pinched nerve can make fingers or toes tingle, feel numb, or go weak. The wrist has a famous one called the **carpal tunnel**. The elbow has one where your "funny bone" is. The ankle has one too.

Doctors find the pinched spot by checking which skin feels numb and which muscles are weak. Rest, splints, or a small surgery can give the nerve room again.
levels.hs:
An **entrapment neuropathy** is damage to a peripheral nerve caused by squeezing at a narrow anatomical passage. Three classic sites are:

- **Carpal tunnel** (wrist): the **median nerve** runs under the **flexor retinaculum** (transverse carpal ligament) alongside nine flexor tendons. Compression causes tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger. Symptoms are often worse at night. Severe cases cause wasting of the **thenar eminence**, the muscle pad at the base of the thumb. This is the most common entrapment neuropathy.
- **Cubital tunnel** (elbow): the **ulnar nerve** passes behind the **medial epicondyle**, the "funny bone." Compression causes numbness in the little finger and half of the ring finger, plus weakness of small hand muscles. It is the second most common entrapment.
- **Tarsal tunnel** (ankle): the **tibial nerve** passes behind the **medial malleolus** under the **flexor retinaculum** of the ankle. Compression causes burning and numbness in the sole of the foot.

Example: a pregnant woman develops night-time numbness in her thumb and fingers. Fluid retention swells the tissues in the carpal tunnel and squeezes the median nerve.

Doctors use **Tinel's sign** (tapping over the nerve causes tingling) and **nerve conduction studies** to confirm the site.
levels.college:
Entrapment occurs where a nerve crosses a fibro-osseous canal with little room to spare. Pressure first impairs blood flow in the small vessels that supply the nerve, then causes focal **demyelination**, and finally **axonal loss**. The deficit maps to the territory beyond the compression point.

**Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS)**
- Boundaries: carpal bones form the floor and walls; the flexor retinaculum forms the roof. It attaches to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally, and to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially.
- Contents: median nerve plus flexor digitorum superficialis (4 tendons), flexor digitorum profundus (4) and flexor pollicis longus (1).
- Deficits: sensory loss over the lateral 3½ digits on the palm side, and **LOAF** weakness (lateral two Lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis superficial head).
- Key point: the **palmar cutaneous branch** of the median nerve passes above the retinaculum, so sensation over the thenar palm is spared. This helps tell CTS apart from a more proximal lesion.
- Tests: Phalen's wrist flexion test, Tinel's sign, Durkan's carpal compression test.
- Risk factors: pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, amyloidosis, repetitive wrist use.

**Cubital tunnel syndrome**
- Roof: **Osborne's ligament** (cubital tunnel retinaculum) and the aponeurosis between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris. Floor: the medial collateral ligament of the elbow.
- Elbow flexion stretches the nerve and raises pressure inside the tunnel.
- Deficits: sensory loss over the medial 1½ digits, including the dorsal hand, because the **dorsal cutaneous branch** arises above the wrist. There is also interosseous weakness, **Froment's sign** and **Wartenberg's sign**.

**Tarsal tunnel syndrome**
- Lies under the flexor retinaculum, between the medial malleolus and the calcaneus.
- Contents, front to back: **"Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry"**: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery and vein, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus.
- Deficits: plantar paresthesia via the medial and lateral plantar nerves. The heel is often spared because the medial calcaneal branches can arise before the tunnel.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the main job is localization: separating entrapment from cervical radiculopathy, a plexus lesion or polyneuropathy. Useful clues:
- **Thenar sensation spared but finger sensation lost** points to the carpal tunnel. A sensory deficit that includes the thenar palm suggests a lesion higher up the median nerve.
- **Dorsal ulnar hand numbness** places an ulnar lesion above the wrist. Sparing of the dorsal hand suggests **Guyon's canal**.
- **Intrinsic weakness with sensory loss extending up the medial forearm** reflects the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, which arises from the medial cord. This suggests a C8/T1 root or lower plexus process, not cubital tunnel.

The **Martin–Gruber anastomosis**, a median-to-ulnar crossover in the forearm found in roughly 15–30% of people, can produce misleading conduction results and spare thenar muscles in ulnar lesions. Read surprising EMG findings with this in mind. Ultrasound is increasingly used alongside EMG. A median nerve cross-sectional area above about 10–12 mm² at the pisiform supports CTS. Ultrasound can also show a nerve subluxing over the medial epicondyle, or a ganglion inside the tarsal tunnel.

Management:
- **CTS**: neutral night splinting and corticosteroid injection help mild disease. Release of the transverse carpal ligament, open or endoscopic, is definitive. The endoscopic approach offers a slightly quicker return to work, but surgeons must keep the **recurrent motor branch** in mind, because its course is variable and sometimes passes through the ligament. Persistent or recurrent symptoms usually mean incomplete release of the distal ligament or a wrong diagnosis.
- **Cubital tunnel**: in situ decompression produces outcomes similar to anterior transposition in randomized trials, with fewer complications. Transposition is reserved for an unstable, subluxing nerve. Severe chronic intrinsic atrophy recovers poorly because motor end plates degenerate after roughly 12–18 months of denervation. This drives interest in **supercharge end-to-side anterior interosseous-to-ulnar motor nerve transfer**.
- **Tarsal tunnel**: surgical results are less reliable than for the upper limb. Identify a mass or structural cause before operating.

Open questions include the true occupational contribution to CTS, whether double crush is real, and how to predict recovery in severe axonal disease.

keyPoints: Entrapment neuropathy is nerve compression in a tight fibro-osseous tunnel
Carpal tunnel: median nerve under the flexor retinaculum, the most common entrapment
Palmar cutaneous branch passes above the retinaculum, so thenar skin is spared in CTS
Cubital tunnel: ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle under Osborne's ligament
Tarsal tunnel: tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus (Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry)
Pressure causes ischemia, then demyelination, then axonal loss, as seen on nerve conduction studies

test.q: Which nerve is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?
test.explain: The median nerve runs through the carpal tunnel with nine flexor tendons. The ulnar nerve travels outside the tunnel, through Guyon's canal.

test.q: Which structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?
test.explain: The flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) spans the carpal arch to form the roof. The carpal bones form the floor and walls.

test.q: Why is sensation over the thenar palm usually spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
choices: The ulnar nerve supplies that skin
The thenar skin is supplied by the C8 dermatome
The radial nerve takes over that skin at night
The palmar cutaneous branch passes above the retinaculum
test.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve before the tunnel and passes superficial to the retinaculum, so carpal tunnel compression does not affect it.

test.q: The cubital tunnel lies behind which bony landmark?
test.explain: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, the 'funny bone,' under Osborne's ligament.

test.q: Numbness over the dorsal ulnar hand suggests an ulnar lesion located:
test.explain: The dorsal cutaneous branch arises above the wrist, so loss of dorsal sensation places the lesion proximal, for example at the elbow.

test.q: Which nerve is compressed in tarsal tunnel syndrome?
test.explain: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum of the ankle.

test.q: Which muscle group weakens in median nerve compression at the wrist?
choices: LOAF muscles of the thenar region
test.explain: LOAF stands for the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis. The others are ulnar- or radial-supplied.

test.q: Why are carpal tunnel symptoms often worse at night?
choices: The median nerve shrinks when the body is cooler
Blood pressure in the hand rises during deep sleep
Flexed wrist sleep postures raise tunnel pressure
Ulnar nerve activity stops during the night
test.explain: Flexing or extending the wrist sharply raises carpal tunnel pressure. That is why neutral night splints help.

test.q: Elbow flexion worsens cubital tunnel syndrome mainly because it:
choices: Stretches the nerve and raises tunnel pressure
Loosens Osborne's ligament around the nerve
Cuts off the radial artery supply to the nerve
Moves the ulnar nerve into the carpal tunnel
test.explain: Flexion lengthens the ulnar nerve and raises cubital tunnel pressure, combining traction with compression.

test.q: What is the name of the sign where tapping over a nerve produces tingling in its territory?
test.explain: Tinel's sign suggests irritation or regeneration of a nerve at the tapped site.

test.q: The roof of the cubital tunnel is formed by ___ ligament.
test.explain: Osborne's ligament, also called the cubital tunnel retinaculum, bridges the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.

test.q: Wasting of the ___ eminence is a sign of severe carpal tunnel syndrome.
test.explain: The thenar muscles at the base of the thumb are supplied by the median nerve's recurrent motor branch.

kidTest.q: What happens in an entrapment neuropathy?
choices: A nerve gets squeezed in a tight space
A muscle turns into a tendon
A bone grows longer than it should
kidTest.explain: The nerve is pinched where it passes through a narrow tunnel.

kidTest.q: Where is the carpal tunnel?
kidTest.explain: The carpal tunnel is in the wrist.

kidTest.q: What can a pinched nerve make your fingers feel?
kidTest.explain: Pinched nerves often cause tingling and numbness.

kidTest.q: Where is the 'funny bone' nerve tunnel?
kidTest.explain: The cubital tunnel is at the elbow, by the funny bone.

kidTest.q: Fill in: a nerve is like a long w _ _ _ carrying messages.
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages like wires carry electricity.

advancedTest.q: A patient has median-territory finger numbness plus numbness over the thenar palm. The most likely interpretation is:
choices: A median lesion proximal to the carpal tunnel
Tarsal tunnel spread from the lower limb
Classic carpal tunnel syndrome at the wrist
advancedTest.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch passes above the retinaculum. Thenar skin involvement implies a lesion before that branch arises, so it is proximal to the tunnel.

advancedTest.q: Intrinsic hand weakness with sensory loss extending up the medial forearm best localizes to:
choices: The C8/T1 root or lower plexus
The cubital tunnel at the elbow
The carpal tunnel at the wrist
advancedTest.explain: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve comes from the medial cord. Its involvement places the lesion proximal to the ulnar nerve itself.

advancedTest.q: Why does chronic severe ulnar neuropathy with long-standing atrophy recover poorly after decompression?
choices: The radial nerve takes over the intrinsics permanently
Osborne's ligament regrows rapidly after surgery
Motor end plates degenerate after prolonged denervation
Schwann cells fail to remyelinate the compressed segment
advancedTest.explain: After roughly 12–18 months of denervation, motor end plates degenerate, which limits recovery and motivates nerve transfers. Demyelination itself is usually repairable by Schwann cells.

advancedTest.q: EMG in an ulnar lesion at the elbow unexpectedly shows sparing of the first dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis. Which variant best explains this?
choices: Bifurcation of the tibial nerve in the tunnel
Palmar cutaneous branch above the retinaculum
advancedTest.explain: In the Martin–Gruber anastomosis, motor fibers destined for ulnar-innervated hand muscles travel with the median nerve above the elbow. They cross to the ulnar nerve in the forearm, distal to the elbow. An ulnar lesion at the elbow can therefore spare muscles such as the first dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis. The anastomosis also confuses conduction studies.
